clue.text: 25 caught drinking, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by word of mouth, so we want what the phrase sounds like rather than its spelling

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
someone drinking is in a bar

explanation.surface: Someone is rumoured to have been caught drinking somewhere they should not.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, C IN A BAR is CINNABAR; the cinnabar is a red-and-black moth whose striped caterpillars eat ragwort.
explanation.definitionFit: The cinnabar moth is a winged creature, so it is an example of the insect named at 25.

clue.text: One such as William Wallace, of course, decapitated

indicators.note: decapitated means the head is cut off, so the first letter of the word is lost

blocks.note: Ascot is a famous racecourse in Berkshire, so a racecourse name answers 'of course'

explanation.surface: A wry aside that William Wallace, being executed, of course lost his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallace really was beheaded, so 'decapitated' seems to describe him; it acts on ASCOT, the racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wallace was a medieval Scottish patriot, so he is one native of Scotland.

clue.text: 25 being its mutant

indicators.note: a mutant is a changed form, so the letters of the little word beside it are altered in order

blocks.note: a man is a human being
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A science-fiction note that some creature exists only as a mutation.
explanation.definitionFit: The mantis is a predatory insect with folded forelegs held as if in prayer.

clue.text: Play game

blocks.note: first meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor of Venice
second meaning: a board game of black and white discs, also called reversi

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the two words look like an instruction to play a game; they are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy shares its title with a two-player board game of flipping counters.

clue.text: US President heading off a lot into kind of republic, endlessly

indicators.note: with its heading off, a word loses its first letter
into tells us one piece goes inside another
endlessly means the final letter of the word before it is dropped

blocks.note: a banana republic is a small unstable state run for a few
much means a lot

explanation.surface: A president heads off with plenty of people into some dubious regime.
explanation.walkthrough: A banana republic is a small unstable state run for a few; two separate deletions trim the pieces before one goes inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: James Buchanan was the fifteenth President of the United States, serving just before Lincoln.

clue.text: Sings, getting drunk and worn

blocks.note: to sing is slang for informing on someone, as is to shop them
oiled is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A singer gets drunk and ends up worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sings' means grasses to the police here, not makes music.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop-soiled goods are slightly damaged or faded from display, so they look worn.

clue.text: Bit of a jumper, holding the record?

definitions.note: describes what the answer does: a thing holding the record

blocks.note: first meaning: the arm part of a jumper, the British word for a sweater
second meaning: the card cover a vinyl record sits in

explanation.surface: Something about a jumper, perhaps an athlete, holding a record.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British sweater, though the surface suggests a record-holding athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: One part of a sweater covers the arm, and a vinyl disc is kept in a card cover of the same name.

clue.text: Wellington, for instance, had to show guile

blocks.note: to air is to show or display
craft means cunning or guile

explanation.surface: The Duke of Wellington needed cunning to win.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vickers Wellington was a Second World War bomber, not the duke.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wellington was a twin-engined RAF bomber, so it is one example of a flying machine.

clue.text: Stand by for armed robbery? On the contrary

indicators.note: on the contrary says the phrase is taken the opposite way round, its back half brought to the front

blocks.note: a hold-up is an armed robbery

explanation.surface: Waiting ready for an armed raid, then saying the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: HOLD-UP becomes UP-HOLD when its two halves trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand by a decision or person is to support it, which is what upholding means.

clue.text: 25 with flavour rolled over

indicators.note: something rolled over is turned upside down, so in a down or across light it reads backwards

blocks.note: a tang is a sharp flavour

explanation.surface: An insect with some flavour gets rolled over.
explanation.definitionFit: The gnat is a small two-winged fly, so it is an example of an insect.

clue.text: 25 on what? In hat?

indicators.note: in tells us the preceding letters sit inside the headgear

blocks.note: re means on or about
eh? is a request to repeat, like what?
a topper is a top hat

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about an insect found sitting in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What?' is the slangy request to repeat yourself, and a topper is the tall formal hat; the question marks hide that both are just wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The treehopper is a sap-sucking bug that leaps among branches, so it is an example of an insect.

clue.text: A Hackney revolutionary at the Guardian? You can count on it!

indicators.note: a revolutionary thing turns round, so the vehicle's name is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a hackney carriage is the formal name for a London taxi
the setter writes for the Guardian, so from its point of view the paper is us

explanation.surface: A rebel from the London borough of Hackney works at the Guardian newspaper, and you can rely on him.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney is a London borough, but a hackney is also a taxi. 'Count on it' is the idiom for relying, used literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A bead frame is a counting device, so it is literally a thing one counts on.

clue.text: 25 sees dog imbibing beverage loudly

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the dog's name takes the drink inside it

blocks.note: a cocker is a cocker spaniel
cha is slang for tea
f is forte, the musical direction for loud

explanation.surface: An insect watches a dog noisily slurping a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockchafer is a large brown beetle, also called the maybug, so it is an example of an insect.

clue.text: Capitalist recluse entertains Spanish gentleman

indicators.note: to entertain is to receive a guest within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a loner keeps to himself
Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A reclusive financier hosts a Spanish nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capitalist' suggests a money man; here it is a resident of the capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living in the capital of England is a resident of that capital city, a quirky reading of capitalist.

clue.text: 25 with long legs, for instance?

definitions.note: describes the game, which has fielders called long leg

blocks.note: first meaning: a chirping jumping insect
second meaning: the bat-and-ball game, whose fielding positions include long leg

explanation.surface: An insect described by its long legs.
explanation.walkthrough: Long leg is a fielding position in cricket, a British bat-and-ball game, so the game is a thing with long legs.
explanation.definitionFit: The chirping grasshopper relative and the bat-and-ball sport share one name.

clue.text: Teatime's wobbly hazard

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady, so the letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Something at teatime is unsteady and dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazard' is a verb, as in hazard a guess, not a danger.
explanation.definitionFit: To hazard a figure is to venture a rough guess at it, which is to give an approximate value.

clue.text: 25 offering 25 to beast

indicators.note: to here means placed against, so one piece is set next to the next

blocks.note: the second 25 is an example of an insect, a small one
a lion is a big beast

explanation.surface: One insect is offered to a beast as a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The same cross-reference does two jobs: first the definition, then an example giving letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The antlion is a winged insect whose larva digs pits to trap ants.

clue.text: 25 continuing to charge 24 down, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the cross-referenced word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: to carry on is to continue
an ion is a particle carrying an electric charge
24 down is FLEA, which is said like flee, meaning to run away

explanation.surface: An insect keeps charging at a flea.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound of FLEA is FLEE, and to flee is to fly in the sense of escaping.
explanation.definitionFit: The onion fly is a small fly whose maggots burrow into onion bulbs, so it is an insect.

clue.text: Taunt outlaw on instrument of torture

indicators.note: in a down light, on means placed above, so the first piece sits atop the next

blocks.note: to outlaw is to bar or forbid
the rack stretched its victims

explanation.surface: Mocking a bandit who has been strapped to a torture device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' is a verb here, not a bandit.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack is to jeer or heckle a speaker or player, which is taunting them.

clue.text: Asian city state crossed by reservists

blocks.note: Cal is a short form for California
to cut across a road is to cross it
the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A city state is invaded by reserve soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City state' looks like one phrase; the city is the definition and the state is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Calcutta, now Kolkata, is a major Indian city on the Hooghly river.

clue.text: Getting on a horse, in German one's restrained

indicators.note: restrained means held in, so the German word is held inside the horse

blocks.note: taken as written
gee-gee is childish slang for a horse
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A German mounting a horse is held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' looks like mounting the horse; it means growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on is an idiom for growing older, which is what ageing describes.

clue.text: European city that's wild and free

blocks.note: mad means wild or crazy
to rid is to free of something

explanation.surface: A city with a reputation for wild, free living.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrid is the capital of Spain, so it is a city in Europe.

clue.text: Mature chap, male not female

indicators.note: male not female says one gender's letter takes the place of the other's

blocks.note: a fellow is a chap
M is the standard abbreviation for male
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A grown-up man, described as male rather than female.
explanation.walkthrough: The F at the front of FELLOW is swapped for M.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow and mature are both used of wine, cheese or people softened and improved by age.

clue.text: 25 thrashing Real 22

indicators.note: a thrashing beats something about, so the words are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
22 across is MADRID

explanation.surface: A football report: someone gives Real Madrid a hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: Real Madrid is a famous Spanish football club, so 'thrashing' reads as a big win.
explanation.definitionFit: The red admiral is a common butterfly with red bands on black wings, so an example of an insect.

clue.text: Consider, some 14s might say, being a spy

definitions.note: a phrase describing the answer, a person who is a spy

indicators.note: some London speakers pronounce th as f, so we want what the word sounds like in that accent

blocks.note: to think is to consider; a Cockney says it with an f

explanation.surface: Think about it, a Londoner might say, being a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 across is LONDONER; many Londoners say f for th, so THINK comes out as FINK.
explanation.definitionFit: A fink is American slang for an informer or stool pigeon, someone who acts as a spy.

clue.text: 25 and caterpillar grub back to front

indicators.note: back to front here means the back letter is moved round to the front

blocks.note: caterpillars feed on leaves, so a leaf is their grub, or food

explanation.surface: An insect and a caterpillar grub get mixed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' is food, not a larva, despite the caterpillar beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The flea is a tiny wingless jumping insect that lives on animals' blood.

clue.text: Creature having been brainwashed?

definitions.note: split as IN SECT, a description of a person

blocks.note: first meaning: a six-legged creepy-crawly
second meaning, read as two words: inside a cult

explanation.surface: A creature that has been brainwashed.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IN SECT: someone brainwashed has joined a sect, or cult.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect is a small six-legged animal, so it is one kind of creature.

clue.text: A hundred left in pretty Devon village

indicators.note: in says the letter goes inside the adjective that follows

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
lovely means pretty
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A hundred of something left behind in a pretty Devon village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' does double duty: part of the definition's picture and the word that holds the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Clovelly is a steep cobbled fishing village on the north coast of Devon, an English county.
